GET /v1/user/:id does db.user.findOne({where:{id:req.params.id}}) with no authentication/authorization; any caller reads arbitrary user's private data (email, password, address, beers) selected purely by attacker-controlled path id.

An HTTP response discloses data the caller is not entitled to receive: GET /v1/user/:id returns the full user record without projection or DTO, and the same source shows user records include a password field, so an authentication credential is disclosed in the HTTP response body.
DELETE /v1/user/:id calls db.user.destroy({where:{id:req.params.id}}) with no auth check; any caller deletes any user object selected by attacker-controlled path id.
An HTTP response construction serializes caught exception detail (raw-object) without normalization, disclosing internal diagnostic information to the client.

Protected data is written to durable storage without encryption or hashing: 'password' is written to durable storage with no hashing anywhere in the value's provenance — the stored verifier is the plaintext password.

A regex with nested ambiguous quantifiers is run over request input here (emailExpression.test/exec). A short crafted string forces exponential backtracking, consuming the single-threaded event loop and denying service to every other request. Rewrite the pattern to remove the nested quantifier, or validate with a non-backtracking matcher.

`handler` completes an account-recovery/verification flow — issuing a session or writing a new password — without ever comparing the submitted proof against the stored secret. The account is selected by an attacker-supplied identifier alone, so anyone who knows the email address can take the account over. Compare the proof in constant time against the stored (hashed) value and require it to be unexpired and single-use.
